chapter.title: Push off and glide

cards.body:
Think of sliding a tray across a wet kitchen counter: one shove, then it slides on by itself. The *glide* is that shove, done on the water-bed. **You push off the wall once, make yourself long and thin like an arrow, and the water carries you** while you do nothing at all.

This is the shape every stroke starts from. Learn it here, and chapters 5 to 7 just add things on top.
cards.simpler:
Picture sliding a tray across a wet counter. One shove, and it slides on by itself. The glide is that shove, done in the water. **You push off the wall once, make your body long and thin like an arrow, and the water carries you** while you do nothing.

Every stroke starts from this shape. Learn it now, and chapters 5 to 7 just add things on top.

cards.prompt: Two friends push off the same wall with the same shove. Priya stretches both arms ahead, hands stacked, face looking at the pool floor. Tom keeps his head up to watch the far wall, arms at his sides. Who glides further?

options.text: Tom. Head up, he can see where he is going and steer.
Priya. Long and thin slips through the water; a lifted head and loose arms drag.
The same. Same wall, same push, same distance.

whyNot.a: That's a wish to see, not a way to glide: a lifted head drops your hips, and dropped hips act like a brake.
whyNot.c: That's only the push. The push is the same, but shape decides how far the push carries you.

cards.reteach: Picture the tray again. Slide it flat and it travels. Tip one end up and it stops dead. Your body on the water works the same way: flat and long goes far, head up and arms out to the sides stops you.

cards.title: Make the arrow first
cards.body:
The glide is a shape before it is a push. Stand in chest-deep water, back to the wall, and make the shape while you are still standing: **both arms stretched ahead, one hand on top of the other, upper arms squeezing your ears**. Swimmers call this *streamline*, which just means the thinnest shape your body can make.

Now the head. Tuck your chin so your face points at the pool floor, not at the far wall. Your head is heavy. Where it goes, your hips follow: head down, hips up, body flat.

Legs together, toes pointed behind you. Now you are an arrow, not a starfish.
cards.simpler:
First the shape, then the push. Stand in chest-deep water, back to the wall, and make the shape while standing: **both arms stretched ahead, one hand on the other, upper arms squeezing your ears**. Swimmers call this streamline, the thinnest shape you can make.

Tuck your chin so your face points at the floor. Your heavy head leads, and your hips follow: head down, hips up, body flat. Legs together, toes pointed. You are an arrow, not a starfish.

cards.title: The quietest 3 metres
cards.body:
Maya, at her first adult lesson, has been told to push off and count until she stops. She puts both feet on the wall, stacks her hands, tucks her chin, and shoves. Then she does nothing, which feels deeply unnatural.

One, two, three, four. She slows, pulls her knees in, and stands. She is nearly 3 metres from the wall. Nobody kicked, nobody paddled. The water did all of it. She says it was the quietest 3 metres of her life.
cards.simpler:
At her first adult lesson, Maya is told to push off and count until she stops. She puts both feet on the wall, stacks her hands, tucks her chin, and shoves. Then she does nothing, which feels strange.

One, two, three, four. She slows, pulls her knees in, and stands. She is nearly 3 metres from the wall. **Nobody kicked and nobody paddled. The water did all of it.** She calls it the quietest 3 metres of her life.

cards.prompt: You push off nicely, but after a second your legs start sinking and you grind to a halt. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Your chin came up to look where you were going, so your hips dropped.
You did not push hard enough off the wall.
You breathed out too early and lost your air.

whyNot.b: That's push strength, which changes how far you go, not whether your legs sink. Sinking legs come from the shape.
whyNot.c: That's chapter 2's breath. Breathing out slowly during a glide is fine; your lungs still hold plenty to keep your chest up.

cards.reteach: Your head is the heaviest thing on the water-bed. Lift it and the other end of you, your hips and legs, goes down to balance it. Face at the floor keeps you flat, and flat is what glides.

cards.title: Then the push, then nothing
cards.body:
Now add the push. Crouch with your shoulders under the water and **both feet flat on the wall, like a frog about to jump**. Arms already stretched ahead before you leave. If you push first and reach second, you lose the glide in the gap.

Push through both feet at once, straight ahead, not upwards. Your face goes in as you go. Breathe out slowly through your nose, as in chapter 2.

Then the hard part: do nothing. No kick, no paddle. Count. When you feel almost still, finish it the chapter 1 way: knees in, hands press down, feet plant, stand. 3 to 5 metres is a good glide.
cards.simpler:
Now add the push. Crouch, shoulders under the water, **both feet flat on the wall, like a frog about to jump**. Stretch your arms ahead before you leave, or you lose the glide. Push through both feet at once, straight ahead, not up. Face in, breathe out slowly through your nose.

Then the hard part: do nothing. No kick, no paddle. Count. When you feel almost still, stand the chapter 1 way. 3 to 5 metres is a good glide.

cards.body:
Dev pushes off well, and the instant his feet leave the tiles he starts windmilling his arms. He is trying to help. He never finds out how far the push alone would have taken him, so he never trusts it, so he keeps windmilling.

Spot it in yourself: **if anything moved before you slowed down, you did not glide**. You swam badly from a standing start. Push, hold the arrow, count, then stand.
cards.simpler:
Dev pushes off well. The moment his feet leave the wall, he starts windmilling his arms. He is trying to help. But he never finds out how far the push alone would take him, so he never trusts it, so he keeps windmilling.

Spot it in yourself: **if anything moved before you slowed down, you did not glide**. You swam badly from a standing start. Push, hold the arrow, count, then stand.

cards.prompt: Which of these is the glide, as this chapter means it?

options.text: Pushing off the wall and kicking hard all the way across the pool.
Pushing off into a long thin shape, face down, and doing nothing until you slow, then standing.
Lying on your back with ears in the water and drifting wherever you end up.

whyNot.a: That's kicking, which is chapter 5. A glide is the stretch of travel before you add anything.
whyNot.c: That's the back float from chapter 3. A glide starts with a push and moves you forward on your front.

cards.reteach: The glide has 3 parts: an arrow shape made before you leave, one push with both feet, and a stretch of doing nothing while the water carries you. Everything that moves after that belongs to a later chapter.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **Make the arrow before you push**: hands stacked, ears squeezed, chin tucked, legs together. Then one shove off the wall with both feet, hold still while the water carries you 3 to 5 metres, and stand the chapter 1 way when you slow.
cards.simpler: **Make the arrow before you push**: hands stacked, ears squeezed, chin tucked, legs together. Then one shove off the wall with both feet. Hold still while the water carries you 3 to 5 metres. When you slow down, stand the chapter 1 way. That is the whole glide.

cards.body: Next time you are in the shallow end: shoulders under, both feet on the wall, arms already out ahead, face down. Push once and count seconds until you stop. Then stand. Write the count down. Beat it tomorrow.
cards.simpler: Next time you are in the shallow end, try this. Shoulders under the water, both feet on the wall, arms already out ahead, face down. **Push once and count the seconds until you stop.** Then stand. Write the number down. Tomorrow, try to beat it.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now push off the wall into a long thin shape and glide 3 to 5 metres with your face in the water, then stand up without grabbing anything.
